title: Review: Indicators; Buffers; Periodic table structure and blocks; Periodic trends
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PT01#t1 term and clue written for the game; AB09#t1 term and clue written for the game; AB08#t2 term and clue written for the game; AB08#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AB08#N.8, AB09#N.13, PT01#N.6, PT02#N.6, AB08#N.7a, AB09#N.4a, PT02#N.12, AB08#N.10b, AB09#N.6a, PT02#N.14, AB09#N.11a, PT02#N.10. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Period
items.clue: A row of the table; its number gives the outer occupied shell.

items.label: Acidic buffer
items.clue: A mixture such as CH₃COOH with CH₃COONa that reduces a change in pH.

items.label: Equivalence point
items.clue: The stage at which acid and base have reacted in the stoichiometric ratio.

items.label: Universal indicator
items.clue: A mixture of several weak acids with different pKa values, used to estimate pH.

questions.stem: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ammonia is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. Which indicator is the most suitable? Ranges: methyl orange 3.1–4.4; phenolphthalein 8.3–10.0; thymol blue 8.0–9.6; alizarin yellow 10.1–12.0.

options.text: phenolphthalein
methyl orange
thymol blue
alizarin yellow

questions.explanation: Strong acid + weak base: NH₄⁺ makes the equivalence point acidic (about pH 5.3), and the steep section runs down to about pH 3.5. Methyl orange changes there.

questions.stem: Inside cells, a buffer of dihydrogenphosphate ions, H₂PO₄⁻, and hydrogenphosphate ions, HPO₄²⁻, helps keep the pH close to 7. A process in the cell releases some OH⁻ ions. Which reaction removes most of the added OH⁻?

options.text: HPO₄²⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) → H₂PO₄⁻(aq)
H₂PO₄⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → HPO₄²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
H₂PO₄⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) → H₃PO₄(aq)
HPO₄²⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → PO₄³⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)

questions.explanation: H₂PO₄⁻ is the weak acid of this pair, so it donates H⁺ to the OH⁻. The ratio [H₂PO₄⁻]/[HPO₄²⁻] changes only slightly, so the pH barely moves.

questions.stem: Germanium is in period 4, group 14. Which is the full electron configuration of a germanium atom?

options.text: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 4p²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d² 4s²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁴

questions.explanation: Period 4, p-block: fill up to 4p. Group 14 gives 14 − 10 = 4 valence electrons, 4s² 4p². With the 3d¹⁰, the total is 32 electrons.

questions.stem: The first ionisation energy of magnesium is lower than that of beryllium. Which explains this?

options.text: Magnesium has more electrons, so the nucleus's pull is shared among more of them.
Magnesium's outer electron is in shell 3, further from the nucleus and more shielded.
Magnesium's 3s electrons are paired, and their repulsion makes one easy to remove.
Magnesium is more reactive, so it gives up its outer electron more readily.

questions.explanation: Mg is [Ne] 3s², Be is 1s² 2s². The extra shell adds distance and shielding, which outweigh the larger nuclear charge (+12 against +4), so less energy is needed.

questions.stem: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (pKa = 4.76) is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) at 298 K. Three indicators are available, with these pH ranges: methyl orange 3.1–4.4; bromothymol blue 6.0–7.6; phenolphthalein 8.3–10.0. Which choice of indicator, with its reason, is correct?

options.text: Phenolphthalein, as the salt CH₃COONa makes the equivalence pH above 7.
Methyl orange, as its range is close to the pKa of ethanoic acid.
Bromothymol blue, as the equivalence point of a titration is at pH 7.
Any of the three, as the pH passes through every range near equivalence.

questions.explanation: At equivalence the flask holds sodium ethanoate; CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻ makes it basic (about pH 8.7). Phenolphthalein's range lies within the steep section.

questions.stem: Which mixture, made up to 1.00 dm³ with water, is an acidic buffer solution?

options.text: HNO₃ (0.10 mol) with NaNO₃ (0.20 mol)
CH₃COOH (0.10 mol) with NaOH (0.20 mol)
NH₃ (0.20 mol) with NH₄Cl (0.10 mol)
CH₃COOH (0.20 mol) with KOH (0.10 mol)

questions.explanation: KOH converts half the acid: CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O, leaving 0.10 mol of each. A weak acid with its conjugate base is an acidic buffer.

questions.stem: Why does silicon have the highest melting point of the Period 3 elements?

options.text: It is a giant covalent lattice, so melting breaks many strong covalent bonds.
Its Si₂ molecules have the strongest London forces in the period.
It has four delocalised electrons per atom, so its metallic bonding is the strongest.
Its atoms have the most electrons in the period, so the forces between them are the strongest.

questions.explanation: Each Si atom is covalently bonded to four others in a giant lattice. All those strong bonds must be broken, which needs far more energy than overcoming London forces or the metallic bonding in Al.

questions.stem: This time 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) is in the flask, and 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid is run in from the burette. The pH curve: 13.0 at the start, 12.0 at 20.5 cm³, 11.0 at 24.5 cm³; then a steep drop through the equivalence point (25.0 cm³, pH 8.7) to 7.2 at 25.1 cm³; then a slow fall to 4.8 at 50.0 cm³. Which indicator should be used?

options.text: alizarin yellow, range 10.1–12.0
methyl orange, range 3.1–4.4
phenolphthalein, range 8.3–10.0
none: the pH falls during this titration, so no indicator gives a sharp end point

questions.explanation: Its whole range lies inside the steep drop, between 24.95 and 25.01 cm³, so one drop changes it, pink to colourless, right at equivalence.

questions.stem: A buffer solution at 298 K contains 0.20 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH and 0.10 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COONa. Ka(CH₃COOH) = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. What is the pH of the buffer?
questions.explanation: [H⁺] = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.20 ÷ 0.10 = 3.48 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³, so pH = 4.46. More acid than salt puts the pH below the pKa.

questions.stem: An argon atom has seven more electrons than a sodium atom, yet argon's first ionisation energy is about three times sodium's. Which explains this?

options.text: Argon's outer shell is full, and a full shell is stable, so it does not want to lose an electron.
Argon has more electrons, so the extra electron–electron repulsion holds its outer electron in place.
Argon's outer electron is in a higher shell than sodium's, so it is held more tightly.
Argon has 18 protons to sodium's 11, and its outer electrons are in the same shell with similar shielding.

questions.stem: A buffer containing 0.20 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH and 0.10 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COO⁻ has pH 4.46. It is diluted with an equal volume of water. To a first approximation, what happens to its pH?

options.text: It rises by about 0.30, as [H⁺] halves when the volume doubles.
It stays at about 4.46, as the ratio [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻] is unchanged.
It rises to pH 7, as the added water neutralises the acid present.
It falls, as dilution makes a larger fraction of CH₃COOH dissociate.

questions.explanation: Both halve (to 0.10 and 0.050 mol dm⁻³), so the ratio stays 2 : 1 and the pH stays 4.46. Dilution does reduce the capacity.

questions.stem: Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine. Which explains this?

options.text: A fluorine atom has more protons than a chlorine atom, so it pulls harder on a shared pair.
Fluorine needs only one electron to fill its outer shell, so it attracts electrons strongly.
In fluorine the shared pair is closer to the nucleus and shielded by fewer inner electrons.
Fluorine releases more energy than chlorine when it gains an electron, so it is more electronegative.

questions.explanation: Fluorine's bonding electrons are in shell 2, shielded only by 1s². Chlorine's are in shell 3, shielded by 10 inner electrons. Shorter distance and less shielding outweigh chlorine's larger nuclear charge.
